opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest change is that robots finally have something like common sense. For decades, robotics was split into two very different problems. One was the low-level problem: how do you walk, how do you grasp, how do you keep your balance. The other was the high-level problem: what should the robot actually do, and how does it understand what a human wants? We made a lot of progress on the first one with control theory, simulation, and reinforcement learning. But the second one was always the bottleneck. Every task had to be hand-specified, and every new environment meant a lot of engineering.

Large language models changed that almost overnight. Suddenly you can say "I spilled my drink, can you help?" and the model understands that it should bring a sponge, not a vacuum. That kind of semantic understanding of the world used to be extremely hard to give a robot, and now it comes almost for free, because these models have absorbed so much human knowledge from the internet.

The second change is in how we build the systems. Before, a robot stack was a pipeline of separate modules for perception, planning, and control, each designed by a different group of people. Now we're moving toward vision-language-action models, where one large model takes in images and language and directly outputs actions. That's a big philosophical shift, from engineering every piece to learning end to end, and it's what lets knowledge from the web transfer into physical behavior. You see robots handle objects or instructions they never saw in their robot training data.

The third change is more cultural. Robotics used to be a relatively small field that moved slowly, because hardware is hard and data is expensive. LLMs brought a lot of attention, talent, and resources into the field, and they gave us a recipe to follow: scale up data, scale up models, and see what emerges. Whether that recipe works for robotics the way it did for language is still an open question, because the physical world is much less forgiving and robot data is far scarcer than text. But for the first time, many of us feel there's a realistic path toward general-purpose robots rather than robots that each do one narrow thing.

So if I had to summarize: LLMs gave robots a brain that understands the world at a semantic level. The remaining challenge, and it's a big one, is connecting that brain to a body that can act reliably and dexterously in the messy real world.

r001.rationale: The response says a person can ask the robot for help in natural language and contrasts this with tasks previously needing hand specification.

r002.rationale: It gives an example of inferring that a sponge is appropriate, but does not describe breaking a high-level instruction into concrete steps.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest change is actually conceptual rather than technical. For a long time, robotics was organized around the idea that every capability had to be engineered or learned from scratch, task by task, robot by robot. Walking, grasping, navigation, manipulation, each one its own research community, its own pipeline, its own data. Large language models broke that assumption. They showed that a single model trained on broad data could carry an enormous amount of general knowledge about the world, and that knowledge turned out to be surprisingly useful for robots.

Concretely, I'd point to three things.

The first is common sense and task understanding. Before LLMs, if you told a robot "clean up the kitchen," it had no idea what that meant. Now a model can decompose that into steps, know that dishes go in the sink and not the trash, understand that a knife should be handled carefully. That high-level semantic layer used to be hand-coded, and now it essentially comes for free.

The second is the interface. Language became the universal API. You can instruct a robot, correct it, ask it why it did something, all in plain language. That changes who can use robots and how fast you can iterate. When I started in this field, programming a robot required a specialist. That barrier is coming down quickly.

The third, and this is the one I find most exciting, is that LLMs changed how we think about scale. They taught the whole community that more diverse data plus a general architecture beats clever hand-designed structure. That lesson is now driving vision-language-action models, where you connect perception, language, and low-level control in one network and train across many robots and tasks. We're still far from the "GPT moment" for robotics, because physical data is scarce and expensive compared to text on the internet. But the recipe is now clear, and the question has shifted from "is this possible" to "how do we get enough of the right data."

I'd add one caveat. Language models are good at knowing what to do, but they're still weak at the physical how. Fine motor control, contact dynamics, reacting in milliseconds, those don't live in text. So the real progress comes from marrying the semantic knowledge in these models with learning methods that are grounded in real physics, whether that's simulation, reinforcement learning, or large-scale teleoperation data. That combination is where I think the field is heading.

r001.rationale: The response says language became the robot’s “universal API,” letting people instruct it in plain language, and contrasts this with specialist robot programming.

r002.rationale: It describes a model decomposing “clean up the kitchen” into steps and presents that ability as part of common-sense task understanding.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change is that large language models give robots access to a much broader base of knowledge. Traditionally, we build a robot for a fairly narrow task, and we put a lot of effort into designing its behavior. With language models, we can start to connect what a person wants, expressed in everyday language, to a sequence of actions the robot might take.

For example, if you say, “Help me clean up the table,” there are many things left unsaid. The robot needs to figure out which objects are dishes, which are trash, where they belong, and what order makes sense. Language models can help with that kind of reasoning and task decomposition. They also make interaction more natural: you can explain a goal, give feedback, or clarify a mistake.

But there is still a big gap between knowing what to do and being able to do it. A model can describe how to pick up a cup, but that doesn’t mean a robot can grasp it reliably without spilling anything. Physical execution requires perception, control, and experience interacting with the world. So I see language models as a very powerful part of the system, while connecting that knowledge to reliable physical skills remains a central challenge.

r001.rationale: It says people can express goals in everyday language and have the robot turn them into actions, contrasting this with the traditional effort of designing behavior for narrow tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes the robot inferring unstated details and deciding which objects to handle and in what order, identifying language-model reasoning and task decomposition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is that large language models give robots access to a much broader base of knowledge about the world. Traditionally, we built a robot to do a specific task, and a lot of the knowledge needed for that task had to be engineered into the system. With language models, we can start to use knowledge learned from text to interpret instructions, break a task into steps, and reason about what to do when something unexpected happens.

They also make it much easier for people to communicate with robots. Instead of specifying every motion, you can describe your goal in natural language. But there is still a big gap between understanding a goal and physically accomplishing it. A model might know that you should pick up a cup before pouring water, but that doesn’t mean it knows how to grasp that particular cup reliably.

So I see language models as a powerful layer for understanding and planning. The challenge is connecting that layer to perception and control, so the robot can ground its decisions in what is actually happening and execute them safely and reliably.

r001.rationale: It says people can describe a goal in natural language instead of specifying every motion, communicating natural-language direction in place of detailed task programming.

r002.rationale: It says language models can break a task into steps, but does not identify that decomposition as commonsense reasoning.
